audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s degree studies how people organise social life, create meaning and respond to change. It combines anthropological theory, social research methods, major electives and supervised ethnographic fieldwork.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options focus on culture and research, identity and inequality, or global change and sustainability. Utrecht provides a longer anthropology sequence and a dedicated progression from ethnographic design to fieldwork and thesis.

curriculum.limitation: This example shows eight compatible major electives, including extended fieldwork. The profiling choices remain open.

componentNotes.ca-bap-2: Complete the 45 EC of compulsory first-year courses and 75 EC of major electives or profiling before this course.
componentNotes.ca-bap-3: Pass BAP 1 and BAP 2 before beginning supervised fieldwork.
componentNotes.ca-choice-fieldwork: This example takes BAP 4 with BAP 3. Taking BAP 3 alone requires agreement with the coordinator.
componentNotes.ca-bap-thesis: Pass BAP 1, 2 and 3. Students write in pairs and receive individual assessments.
componentNotes.ca-profiling: Choose 45 EC, with at least 15 EC at intermediate level or above.

notes.text: Utrecht has a dedicated ethnographic sequence from methods and research design to supervised fieldwork and a thesis written in pairs. UCR offers qualitative research, and the closest option adds research statistics. The UCR options draw on different disciplines to study related social questions.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

GOSSOCI111.text: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
